sections.h2: How much can a New York landlord collect as a security deposit?
sections.html:
One month's rent is the ceiling for most dwellings. General Obligations Law section 7-108(1-a) bars any deposit or advance above that amount, with carve-outs for seasonal units, owner-occupied co-op apartments and a few other housing types such as assisted living. The rule applies in the statute to non-rent-stabilized units and cannot be waived in a lease.

The whole deposit comes back to the tenant on move-out, less reasonable and itemized costs for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear, unpaid utilities owed to the landlord and moving or storage of belongings. Ordinary wear and damage left by a prior tenant cannot be charged.

  • Before move-in, the landlord must offer a walk-through with the tenant, and if the tenant asks, both sign a written condition report.
  • Before move-out, the landlord must tell the tenant of the right to an inspection, held one to two weeks before the tenancy ends, with 48 hours' written notice.
  • Within 14 days after the tenant leaves, the landlord must send an itemized statement and the balance. Miss that deadline and the right to keep any part of the deposit is gone.
  • In a dispute the landlord has to prove the amount kept was reasonable, and a willful violation can bring punitive damages up to twice the deposit.

sections.h2: Who is responsible for the tenant's deposit when a landlord sells?
sections.html:
The buyer can end up owing it. If the old landlord does not hand the deposit over, section 7-108(2) makes the new owner liable for the deposit plus interest whenever the buyer had actual knowledge of it. Knowledge is presumed in three situations.

When a buyer is treated as knowing about a tenant deposit, General Obligations Law 7-108(2)
SituationWhat follows
Deposit placed in a bank in the six months before closingBuyer is deemed to know of it
Deposit acknowledged in a lease in effect at closingBuyer is deemed to know of it
Tenant supplies a cancelled check, receipt or signed lease from a prior ownerBuyer is deemed to know of it
No record of a deposit anywhereBuyer must send written notice within 30 days after closing, and the tenant has 30 days to show proof

Source: New York State Senate, Open Legislation.

A buyer who finds no record can demand that the seller set up an escrow account equal to one month's rent to cover a late claim. Sellers who keep clean deposit records and give the buyer copies at closing avoid that argument entirely.

sections.h2: How much notice must a landlord give for a rent increase or non-renewal?
sections.html:
When the rent goes up by 5 percent or more, or the landlord will not renew, written notice is required, and its length depends on how long the tenant has lived there. Real Property Law section 226-c sets 30 days for under one year of occupancy, 60 days for one to two years and 90 days for more than two years or a lease of at least two years. The longer of the tenant's total time in the home or the length of the lease governs.

If a landlord gives late notice, the tenancy continues on its existing terms from the day written notice arrives until the full notice period has run. Under the version in force until June 15, 2034, the notice must also say whether the unit falls under Article 6-A, the good cause eviction law, and if it is exempt, why.

Section 214 lists the exemptions. They include owner-occupied buildings with no more than ten units, small landlords who disclose their ownership, condominium and cooperative units, rent-regulated units and homes with a certificate of occupancy issued on or after January 1, 2009 for thirty years. Section 214 also refers to local laws adopted by villages, towns and cities outside New York City, so ask the local clerk whether yours has one.

sections.h2: What does the warranty of habitability require?
sections.html:
Every residential lease, written or oral, carries an implied promise from the landlord that the home and the common areas are fit to live in. Real Property Law section 235-b says occupants may not be subjected to conditions dangerous, hazardous or harmful to life, health or safety, and any waiver by the tenant is void.

  • A condition caused by the tenant or someone under the tenant's direction is not a breach.
  • A court assessing damages does not need expert testimony.
  • For rent-regulated homes, damages are reduced by any rent reduction already ordered by the state housing agency for the same problem.

For a seller, the warranty applies to every residential lease in the building, so open repair complaints are worth sorting out before listing.

sections.h2: Can a landlord evict without going to court?
sections.html:
No. Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law section 711 says no tenant or lawful occupant of a dwelling may be removed except in a special proceeding. The same section defines a squatter as a person who enters or stays on property without the owner's permission or any right, and says a squatter is not a tenant.

The common grounds are a tenant staying after the lease ends and a tenant who has defaulted on rent. For unpaid rent, the landlord must serve a written demand giving at least 14 days to pay or leave, and the notice must follow the service rules in section 735. Until June 15, 2034, that notice also has to carry the Article 6-A disclosure described above.

Two smaller duties often come up in nonpayment cases. Under section 235-e, a landlord taking cash or any payment other than the tenant's personal check must give a written receipt with the date, amount, premises and period covered, and signature and title. If rent is not received within five days of the due date, the landlord must send a notice by certified mail, and skipping it is an affirmative defense for the tenant in a nonpayment case.

sections.h2: Does a tenant who moves out early still owe rent?
sections.html:
Often the answer is partly. Real Property Law section 227-e requires a landlord whose tenant leaves in breach of the lease to act in good faith and take reasonable, customary steps to re-rent at fair market value or the old rent, whichever is lower. When a new tenant's lease starts, it ends the earlier lease and reduces what the first tenant owes.

The party asking for damages carries the burden of proof, and a lease clause that excuses the landlord from mitigating is void as against public policy. A landlord who is also thinking about selling should keep records of advertising and showings, since they are the evidence a court will want.

sections.h2: How should an owner prepare to sell a New York rental?
sections.html:
Start with paper. Gather every lease, the deposit records and the dates of the last rent notices, because the buyer's attorney will ask for them and a buyer can be liable for any deposit it knew about. Check rent receipts, since a gap in receipts can matter if a nonpayment case follows.

  • Confirm whether any unit is rent-regulated or exempt from the good cause law, and note the reason.
  • Do not try to remove a tenant yourself. A special proceeding in court is required.
  • Time any non-renewal or rent notice to the 30, 60 or 90 day schedule so it does not become an argument at closing.
  • Resolve habitability complaints in writing, since they carry over to the buyer.

Rent-regulated homes follow separate laws, which the statutes name as the rent stabilization law, the city rent and rehabilitation law and the emergency housing rent control law. Ask your attorney which regime covers your building.

faqs.q: What is the maximum security deposit in New York?
faqs.a: One month's rent for most dwellings. The cap comes from General Obligations Law section 7-108(1-a), which lists exceptions such as seasonal units and owner-occupied co-op apartments.

faqs.q: How fast must a landlord return a deposit?
faqs.a: Within 14 days after the tenant has moved out, with an itemized statement of any deductions. A landlord who misses the deadline gives up the right to keep any part of it.

faqs.q: How much notice is needed for a New York rent increase?
faqs.a: For an increase of 5 percent or more, 30 days if the tenant has lived there under a year, 60 days for one to two years and 90 days beyond that, under Real Property Law section 226-c.

faqs.q: Can a buyer be held liable for a deposit the seller kept?
faqs.a: Yes, when the buyer had actual knowledge of it. Deposits in a bank within six months of closing or named in a lease then in force count as known to the buyer.

faqs.q: Who counts as a squatter in New York?
faqs.a: A person who enters or stays on property with no permission, title or right. Under RPAPL section 711, a squatter is not a tenant, though a lawful tenant can only be removed through a special proceeding.
